## What you will learn

After working through this tutorial, you should be able to:

- derive active power and power factor from sinusoidal voltage and current;
- connect the power factor to complex power and the power triangle;
- distinguish leading, lagging, displacement, and true power factor;
- explain why a low power factor increases current for a fixed active-power transfer;
- calculate a shunt capacitor for a simple single-phase inductive load; and
- recognise when the familiar formula $\mathrm{pf}=\cos\phi$ is not sufficient.

## Prerequisites

You should be comfortable with sinusoidal waveforms and RMS values. The [complex-numbers tutorial](complex-numbers-in-ac-circuits.qmd) explains phasors, impedance, and complex power in more detail. Here we build on those ideas to focus on the physical and practical meaning of power factor.

## 1. Active power is only part of the current story

An AC source may need to supply current even when not all of the associated energy is converted into heat, light, or mechanical work. Inductors and capacitors store energy during part of a cycle and return it later. This exchange contributes to RMS current and equipment loading, but its average energy transfer over a complete cycle is zero.

Power factor compares the average active power $P$ with the voltage-current loading:

$$
\mathrm{pf}
=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}}.
$$ {#eq-pf-general-definition}

For an absorbing load with $P\ge 0$, the magnitude lies between zero and one. A value near one means that most of the available voltage-current product contributes to average power transfer. A lower value means that more current is required for the same active power at the same voltage.

Rearranging @eq-pf-general-definition gives

$$
I_{\mathrm{rms}}
=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}\mathrm{pf}}.
$$ {#eq-pf-current-for-power}

This relation is why power factor matters to conductors, transformers, generators, converters, and switchgear: they must carry or interrupt current and are commonly limited by voltage and current rather than active power alone.

::: {.callout-note}
Some conventions use a signed power factor when power reverses direction. Others report a nonnegative magnitude together with a **leading** or **lagging** label. This tutorial considers an absorbing load and uses the second convention unless stated otherwise.
:::

## 2. Derive power factor from two sinusoids

Consider a sinusoidal voltage and current at the same angular frequency $\omega$:

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{2}V\cos(\omega t+\theta_v),
\qquad
i(t)=\sqrt{2}I\cos(\omega t+\theta_i),
$$ {#eq-pf-sinusoidal-waveforms}

where $V$ and $I$ are RMS magnitudes. Define the voltage-current phase difference as

$$
\phi=\theta_v-\theta_i.
$$ {#eq-pf-phase-difference}

Using $2\cos a\cos b=\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b)$, the instantaneous power is

$$
p(t)=VI\left[
\cos\phi
+\cos(2\omega t+\theta_v+\theta_i)
\right].
$$ {#eq-pf-instantaneous-power}

The second term oscillates at twice the electrical frequency and has zero average over a complete period. The active power is therefore

$$
P=VI\cos\phi.
$$ {#eq-pf-active-power}

Substitution into @eq-pf-general-definition gives the sinusoidal result

$$
\mathrm{pf}=\cos\phi.
$$ {#eq-pf-cosine}

The phase angle, not a delay measured in seconds, is what stays meaningful when the frequency is specified. A fixed time delay corresponds to a different phase angle if the frequency changes.

## 3. Complex power and the power triangle

With cosine-based RMS phasors and the passive sign convention, absorbed complex power is [@grainger1994]

$$
\underline S
=\underline V\underline I^*
=P+\mathrm{j}Q.
$$ {#eq-pf-complex-power}

For the sinusoidal waveforms in @eq-pf-sinusoidal-waveforms,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= VI\cos\phi,\\
Q &= VI\sin\phi,\\
|\underline S| &= VI=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pf-power-components}

Active power $P$ is measured in watts, reactive power $Q$ in var, and apparent power $|\underline S|$ in volt-amperes. The units distinguish different physical roles even though all three have the same underlying dimensions.

Under the stated convention, the sign of $Q$ identifies the phase relationship for an absorbing load:

| Load behaviour | Current relative to voltage | $\phi=\theta_v-\theta_i$ | Reactive power | Label |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Inductive | lags | $>0$ | $Q>0$ | lagging |
| Resistive | in phase | $=0$ | $Q=0$ | unity |
| Capacitive | leads | $<0$ | $Q<0$ | leading |

: Phase and reactive-power signs under the passive sign convention {#tbl-pf-leading-lagging}

The scalar $\cos\phi$ alone cannot distinguish $+\phi$ from $-\phi$. A complete report therefore gives both a power-factor magnitude and a leading or lagging label, or gives the signs of $P$ and $Q$ explicitly.

## 4. Why a lower power factor increases losses and ratings

Suppose a line with resistance $R_{\ell}$ delivers fixed active power $P$ at fixed RMS voltage $V$. From @eq-pf-current-for-power, its resistive loss is

$$
P_{\mathrm{loss}}
=I^2R_{\ell}
=\left(\frac{P}{V\,\mathrm{pf}}\right)^2R_{\ell}.
$$ {#eq-pf-line-loss}

Reducing the power factor from $1.0$ to $0.8$ increases current by a factor of $1/0.8=1.25$ and line loss by a factor of $1/0.8^2=1.5625$, if every other quantity in this comparison remains fixed. The larger current also causes a larger series voltage drop and consumes more of a device's ampere or volt-ampere capability.

This does **not** mean that power factor and efficiency are the same quantity. An ideal inductor has zero power factor and zero average power loss; a real motor can have a high power factor while still dissipating substantial losses. Power factor describes how voltage and current combine at a terminal. Efficiency compares useful output power with active input power.

## 5. Worked inductive-load example

Connect an impedance

$$
\underline Z=12+\mathrm{j}9\ \Omega
$$

to a $230\ \mathrm{V}$ RMS, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ source. The impedance magnitude is $15\ \Omega$ and its angle is $36.87^\circ$, so the current should lag the voltage and the power factor should be $12/15=0.8$.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pf-inductive-load
#| lst-cap: "Calculate power and current for an inductive load"
#| code-summary: "Calculate complex power, power factor, and line loss"

import numpy as np

frequency = 50.0  # Hz
voltage = 230.0 + 0.0j  # V RMS
load_impedance = 12.0 + 9.0j  # ohm
line_resistance = 0.40  # ohm

current = voltage / load_impedance
complex_power = voltage * current.conjugate()
active_power = complex_power.real
reactive_power = complex_power.imag
apparent_power = abs(complex_power)
power_factor = active_power / apparent_power

unity_pf_current = active_power / abs(voltage)
actual_line_loss = abs(current) ** 2 * line_resistance
unity_pf_line_loss = unity_pf_current**2 * line_resistance

print(f"I = {abs(current):.3f} A at {np.rad2deg(np.angle(current)):+.2f} deg")
print(f"S = {active_power:.2f} {reactive_power:+.2f}j VA")
print(f"|S| = {apparent_power:.2f} VA")
print(f"power factor = {power_factor:.3f} lagging")
print(f"current at unity power factor for the same P = {unity_pf_current:.3f} A")
print(f"line loss at actual power factor = {actual_line_loss:.2f} W")
print(f"line loss at unity power factor = {unity_pf_line_loss:.2f} W")
print(f"loss ratio = {actual_line_loss / unity_pf_line_loss:.4f}")
```

The load absorbs about $2.82\ \mathrm{kW}$ and $2.12\ \mathrm{kvar}$ while requiring $3.53\ \mathrm{kVA}$. Its $15.33\ \mathrm{A}$ current exceeds the $12.27\ \mathrm{A}$ that would transfer the same active power at unity power factor. The printed line-loss ratio verifies the $1/\mathrm{pf}^2$ scaling for this controlled comparison.

::: {.callout-tip}
Change the reactance from `9.0j` to `-9.0j` before rerunning. The current magnitude and power-factor magnitude stay the same, but the current becomes leading and the sign of reactive power reverses.
:::

## 6. Correct a lagging power factor with a shunt capacitor

A capacitor connected in parallel with an inductive load can supply negative reactive power locally. The load still absorbs the same $P$ and $Q$ in this idealised calculation, but the source supplies only their sum with the capacitor contribution.

For an initial angle $\phi_1$ and a desired lagging angle $\phi_2$ at the same active power,

$$
Q_1=P\tan\phi_1,
\qquad
Q_2=P\tan\phi_2.
$$

The required capacitor reactive power is

$$
Q_C=Q_2-Q_1.
$$ {#eq-pf-capacitor-reactive-power}

For a single-phase shunt capacitor across RMS voltage $V$,

$$
Q_C=-\omega C V^2,
\qquad
C=-\frac{Q_C}{\omega V^2}.
$$ {#eq-pf-capacitance}

Use @eq-pf-capacitance to raise the source power factor of the worked load from $0.80$ lagging to $0.95$ lagging.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pf-capacitor-correction
#| lst-cap: "Size a single-phase shunt correction capacitor"
#| code-summary: "Correct the source power factor from 0.80 to 0.95"

target_power_factor = 0.95
target_angle = np.arccos(target_power_factor)
target_reactive_power = active_power * np.tan(target_angle)
capacitor_reactive_power = target_reactive_power - reactive_power

omega = 2.0 * np.pi * frequency
capacitance = -capacitor_reactive_power / (omega * abs(voltage) ** 2)

corrected_complex_power = active_power + 1j * target_reactive_power
corrected_source_current = np.conjugate(corrected_complex_power / voltage)
corrected_power_factor = active_power / abs(corrected_complex_power)

print(f"initial source Q = {reactive_power:.2f} var")
print(f"target source Q = {target_reactive_power:.2f} var")
print(f"capacitor Q = {capacitor_reactive_power:.2f} var")
print(f"capacitance = {capacitance * 1e6:.2f} microfarad")
print(f"corrected source current = {abs(corrected_source_current):.3f} A")
print(f"corrected source power factor = {corrected_power_factor:.3f} lagging")
print(
    "reactive-power balance residual = "
    f"{abs(reactive_power + capacitor_reactive_power - target_reactive_power):.3e} var"
)
```

The capacitor supplies part of the load's reactive-power demand, reducing the source current while leaving the ideal load unchanged. Correcting exactly to unity is not always the best practical target: load variation can produce overcorrection, and a capacitor can interact with network inductance to create resonance or amplify harmonics.

::: {.callout-warning}
@Eq-pf-capacitance is a single-phase formula for a capacitor directly across the stated voltage. Three-phase capacitor-bank formulas depend on whether the elements are connected in star or delta and on whether the stated voltage is phase-to-neutral or line-to-line. The [star-and-delta tutorial](star-delta-three-phase-systems.qmd) develops those voltage relations.
:::

## 7. Displacement power factor is not always true power factor

@Eq-pf-cosine assumes sinusoidal voltage and current at one frequency. For arbitrary periodic waveforms, the true power factor remains

$$
\mathrm{pf}_{\mathrm{true}}
=\frac{\dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T v(t)i(t)\,\mathrm dt}
{V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}}.
$$ {#eq-pf-true-waveform}

If the voltage is sinusoidal but the current contains harmonics, let $I_1$ be the RMS magnitude of its fundamental component and let $\phi_1$ be the phase displacement between the voltage and that component. Orthogonal current harmonics raise total RMS current without contributing active power against an ideal fundamental-frequency voltage. In that case,

$$
\mathrm{pf}_{\mathrm{true}}
=\underbrace{\cos\phi_1}_{\text{displacement factor}}
\underbrace{\frac{I_1}{I_{\mathrm{rms}}}}_{\text{distortion factor}}.
$$ {#eq-pf-displacement-distortion}

The next example combines a $10\ \mathrm{A}$ fundamental current lagging by $30^\circ$ with a $5\ \mathrm{A}$ third harmonic.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pf-distorted-current
#| lst-cap: "Compare displacement and true power factor"
#| code-summary: "Calculate power factor for a current containing a third harmonic"

sample_count = 20_000
time = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0 / frequency, sample_count, endpoint=False)

voltage_waveform = np.sqrt(2.0) * 230.0 * np.cos(omega * time)
fundamental_current_rms = 10.0
third_harmonic_current_rms = 5.0
fundamental_lag = np.deg2rad(30.0)

current_waveform = np.sqrt(2.0) * (
    fundamental_current_rms * np.cos(omega * time - fundamental_lag)
    + third_harmonic_current_rms * np.cos(3.0 * omega * time + np.deg2rad(20.0))
)

voltage_rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(voltage_waveform**2))
current_rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(current_waveform**2))
waveform_active_power = np.mean(voltage_waveform * current_waveform)
true_power_factor = waveform_active_power / (voltage_rms * current_rms)
displacement_factor = np.cos(fundamental_lag)
distortion_factor = fundamental_current_rms / current_rms

print(f"V_rms = {voltage_rms:.3f} V")
print(f"I_rms = {current_rms:.3f} A")
print(f"active power = {waveform_active_power:.3f} W")
print(f"displacement factor = {displacement_factor:.4f}")
print(f"distortion factor = {distortion_factor:.4f}")
print(f"true power factor = {true_power_factor:.4f}")
print(f"factor-product residual = {abs(true_power_factor - displacement_factor * distortion_factor):.3e}")
```

The displacement factor is about $0.866$, but the true power factor is only about $0.775$ because the harmonic current increases total RMS current. A capacitor chosen only from the fundamental-frequency phase angle can improve displacement power factor without removing harmonic distortion.

## 8. Practical pitfalls

### Treating power factor as efficiency

Power factor concerns terminal voltage, current, and active power. Efficiency concerns active-power losses between input and useful output. Neither determines the other.

### Omitting the sign convention

The labels leading, lagging, absorbed, and supplied depend on the defined current direction and voltage polarity. State the convention before interpreting $Q$ or comparing formulas.

### Applying $\cos\phi$ to distorted waveforms

$\cos\phi$ is the displacement power factor for sinusoidal quantities. Use @eq-pf-general-definition with total RMS values and average active power when distortion is present.

### Correcting a varying load with one fixed capacitor

A capacitor that is appropriate at rated load may overcorrect at light load. Switched banks, converter-based compensation, or coordinated control may be needed when operating conditions vary.

### Assuming a low power factor always means large reactive power

Harmonic distortion can lower true power factor even when the fundamental reactive power is small. Inspect both phase displacement and waveform distortion.

## 9. Takeaways

- Power factor is active power divided by RMS voltage-current loading.
- For single-frequency sinusoids, $\mathrm{pf}=\cos(\theta_v-\theta_i)$.
- Under the passive sign convention, an inductive load absorbs positive reactive power and has lagging current; a capacitive load has the opposite signs.
- For fixed active power and voltage, lower power factor means higher current and therefore higher resistive line loss.
- Shunt compensation changes the reactive power seen by the source, but its connection, voltage, operating range, and resonance risk all matter.
- With distorted waveforms, true power factor includes both displacement and distortion effects.

The [effective-value tutorial](effective-rms-value-in-ac-circuits.qmd) develops the RMS quantities used throughout this article. The [complex-numbers tutorial](complex-numbers-in-ac-circuits.qmd) continues from the same equations to impedance, RLC circuits, and frequency response.
